metaDescription: Five budget impact wrenches under $150 compared on honest torque, battery setup and drive size, with a plain look at inflated torque claims.
expertTake: The AOBEN 1/2-inch brushless kit is the best balanced pick: a believable 450 ft-lbs claim, variable speed ranges and a 4Ah battery. The SEYVUM is the low-cost alternative with a similar claim, and the Eastvolt corded wrench is the pick if you never leave a garage with an outlet. Treat every torque figure here as a marketing peak. If you wrench on rusted truck lug nuts weekly, a name-brand tool is the only safe buy.
introParagraphs: An impact wrench is a hammer-and-anvil tool that delivers rotational blows to a nut, which lets a small motor loosen a stuck fastener that a ratchet would fight. The box torque figures at low prices are rarely comparable, because they quote different things and some are simply too large to be real.
This guide explains how to read those numbers, which compromises are harmless for a homeowner and which ones leave you stuck with a seized lug nut.

products.name: AOBEN 1/2 in Brushless Cordless Impact Wrench Kit
products.description:
The AOBEN is the most sensible kit in this group because its numbers are plausible for a 20V-class brushless tool. A claim of 450 ft-lbs of peak torque is about what mid-priced brushless 1/2-inch wrenches quote, and the three speed ranges, up to 2,400 RPM, let you drive a lug nut gently and not slam it. A built-in LED lights the nut in a dark wheel well.

The all-copper brushless motor wastes less energy as heat than a brushed one, which matters when a 4Ah pack feeds a tool that draws high current. Compared with the SEYVUM at a similar 650 N.m claim, the AOBEN lists the lower figure and the clearer speed ranges. Against the Seesii at 665 ft-lbs, it is rated lower, but honest torque is not the same as high torque.

Ownership advice: a wrench like this removes lug nuts that are tightened to 80 to 100 ft-lbs with ease, so it suits a spare tire or seasonal swap. Always torque lug nuts to spec with a hand wrench or a torque stick, because an impact will overtighten them and warp rotors. Keep the socket set for impact use, since chrome sockets can shatter.
products.bestFor: Homeowners who swap tires seasonally and want a believable, balanced tool.
pros: 4Ah battery lasts a few wheel swaps
cons: Peak torque is a maker claim

products.name: SEYVUM 20V 1/2 in Cordless Impact Wrench
products.description:
The SEYVUM is a 20V wrench with a claimed 650 N.m, or about 480 ft-lbs, of peak torque. The maker says the motor design takes 33 percent less space and runs cooler, and the trigger gives infinite speed control, so the harder you pull the faster it spins. Sockets ship in the box, which means you can use it the day it arrives.

At 480 ft-lbs it claims about 7 percent more than the AOBEN's 450, which is within the margin of marketing noise. The practical difference is the kit: the SEYVUM comes with a battery and sockets, and the AOBEN has a more detailed speed range. If you want the lowest outlay for a tool that handles lug nuts and stuck bolts, this is a safe choice.

For ownership, treat the supplied sockets as light-duty and replace them with impact-rated ones if you plan regular use. Let the tool rest after a minute of continuous hammering, because a small motor builds heat fast, and a hot battery pack will cut out before the motor does. Torque lug nuts by hand on final tightening so wheel studs do not stretch.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want the lowest outlay for a working wheel and bolt tool.
cons: Torque figure is peak, not working

products.name: Seesii 1/2 in Brushless Impact Wrench with Two 4Ah Batteries
products.description:
The Seesii leads the group on paper. It lists 665 ft-lbs of loosening torque, 579 ft-lbs of tightening torque, 3,300 impacts per minute and two 4Ah batteries. Having two batteries is the practical highlight, since one charges while the other works.

Those numbers need perspective. Loosening torque is a peak breakaway figure, usually higher than the tightening number, and it is measured differently from brand to brand. Next to the AOBEN at 450 ft-lbs, the Seesii's claim is about 48 percent higher, but a bigger number on a small tool with a small battery is not the same as better performance on a rusted nut. The ultra-thick 1/2-inch square head is the kind of detail that suggests the tool is built to take the hammering.

Ownership comes down to the batteries and the brand. Two 4Ah packs give you real working time on a weekend of wheel changes, and you can leave one on the charger. Parts, service and long-term battery supply are weaker than with a major brand, so plan to replace the kit instead of repairing it.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want two batteries and the biggest claimed torque in the group.
cons: Claims are not comparable across brands

products.name: Eastvolt 800W Corded 1/2 in Impact Wrench
products.description:
The Eastvolt trades a battery for a cord. A 7.5-amp, 800-watt motor spins up to 3,400 RPM and strikes 3,700 times per minute, with a claimed maximum torque of 450 ft-lbs. That matches the AOBEN's 450 ft-lbs claim, but a wall outlet gives it constant power with no fade as a battery would.

A corded impact has no battery to age out, and its price reflects it. The real limits are the cord and the vibration: a corded universal motor has brushes that wear, and the tool is louder and heavier than a brushless 20V one. In a home garage, those are small prices to pay for unlimited runtime.

Use it for lug nuts, trailer hitches, rusted bolts and deck lag screws, and keep the cord clear of the socket. The forward and reverse rocker switch is easy to reach. If you only work at home near an outlet, this is the most durable pick here, and if you work at a roadside, buy a cordless one.
products.bestFor: Garage owners who work near an outlet and do not want to manage batteries.
cons: Louder and heavier than brushless cordless

products.name: Kwionsi 12V 1/2 in Brushless Impact Wrench
products.description:
The Kwionsi is a compact 12V-class tool, with a claimed 110 ft-lbs of torque, brushless motor and a built-in 2,000 mAh battery. It is the small, light tool for bolts, bike and lawn equipment, patio furniture and light automotive work. The built-in battery means no removable pack to buy or lose.

Its torque is about a quarter of the AOBEN's 450 ft-lbs claim, so it is not a lug-nut tool. A lug nut tightened to the typical wheel spec will not break loose reliably with 110 ft-lbs. What it does well is nuts and bolts in the 10 to 22 mm range where a ratchet is slow and a full-size impact is overkill.

Ownership is simple: charge over USB-C, store it with the battery partly charged, and keep it away from wet ground. Because the battery is built in, a failing cell means a failed tool. Do not use it as a breaker bar for stubborn bolts, because the small anvil and gearbox are sized for a fraction of the torque of the bigger tools. If you want a tool for small jobs and not tires, this is the right size.
products.bestFor: People who want a small impact wrench for bikes, lawn gear and light automotive jobs.
pros: Light and compact for tight spaces
Brushless motor with 3,200 RPM top speed
USB-C charging, no extra pack to buy
cons: 110 ft-lbs will not break lug nuts reliably

buyingCriteria.explanation: Impact wrench torque is quoted as a peak breakaway figure, and at this price those numbers are marketing. A believable claim for a 20V-class 1/2-inch brushless wrench is about 300 to 500 ft-lbs, which fits the AOBEN at 450 and the SEYVUM at 480. A claim far above that on a tool the size of a drill is a red flag. Use the number to rank tools within the same brand tier, not to promise a stuck nut will move. Ask what the claim measures, because a tightening figure and a loosening figure for the same tool can differ by 15 percent or more, as the Seesii's two numbers show.

A 1/2-inch drive is the standard for lug nuts and automotive work. A 3/8-inch drive is lighter and suits smaller fasteners, and a 3/4-inch drive is for heavy equipment. All five tools here use 1/2-inch square drives, so sockets are interchangeable. Buy impact-rated sockets, not chrome ones. Chrome vanadium sockets are hard and brittle, and under hammer blows they can split and throw fragments, whereas impact sockets use softer chrome-molybdenum steel that deforms instead of shattering.

An impact wrench pulls high current in short bursts, so a 2Ah pack can sag under load while a 4Ah pack holds up. The Seesii includes two 4Ah batteries, and the Eastvolt avoids the question with a cord. A wheel swap uses a few minutes of trigger time, so one 4Ah pack covers a whole car. A 2Ah pack will also do it, but cold weather cuts lithium output noticeably, so the larger pack is the safer choice in a winter driveway.

Brushless motors waste less heat and last longer, which matters on a tool that is run in short, hard bursts. The AOBEN, Seesii and Kwionsi are brushless, and the Eastvolt uses a brushed universal motor. For rare use, either is fine.

A tool with variable speed ranges lets you start nuts gently so they do not cross-thread. The AOBEN has three ranges up to 2,400 RPM. A single-speed tool can strip a stud on the first hit. Run a nut on by hand for a turn or two before the impact takes over, whatever the tool.

Small brands rarely stock parts. A fresh battery in three years may not exist. Treat the tool as a consumable, and keep the box for returns. Before you commit, check that the battery model is sold separately, since a tool with an orphaned battery is a tool with a short life.

specDecoder.meaning: The peak torque a tool can apply to loosen a fastener, usually the biggest number on the box. The Seesii claims 665 ft-lbs of it.
specDecoder.watchFor: It is measured differently by each brand, so compare it only within a brand tier.

specDecoder.meaning: The torque a tool can apply while tightening, usually lower than breakaway. The Seesii lists 579 ft-lbs of it.
specDecoder.watchFor: A wrench with no fastening figure may be hiding a lower working torque.

specDecoder.meaning: How many hammer blows the tool delivers each minute. The Eastvolt is rated at 3,700 and the Seesii at 3,300.
specDecoder.watchFor: Higher IPM helps stuck nuts, but only if the blow energy is high enough.

specDecoder.meaning: 1 N.m equals about 0.74 ft-lbs. The SEYVUM's 650 N.m is about 480 ft-lbs.
specDecoder.watchFor: Some ads mix units so that a big N.m number looks like a big ft-lb number.

specDecoder.meaning: A motor with electronic switching and no carbon brushes. It runs cooler and lasts longer.
specDecoder.watchFor: It does not mean more torque by itself.

howWeEvaluated.title: Plausibility of torque claims
howWeEvaluated.description: We converted every torque claim to ft-lbs and compared it with what a 20V-class 1/2-inch tool can plausibly deliver. We ranked the AOBEN and SEYVUM as believable, and treated higher claims with caution.

howWeEvaluated.title: Battery setup
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared battery capacity and count, noting that the Seesii ships with two 4Ah packs and the Kwionsi has a built-in 2,000 mAh cell.

howWeEvaluated.title: Motor type
howWeEvaluated.description: We separated brushless tools from the Eastvolt's brushed corded motor, and weighed efficiency against simplicity.

howWeEvaluated.title: Speed control
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at speed ranges and trigger control because gentle starts prevent cross-threading and stripped studs.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit for the cap
howWeEvaluated.description: Every tool has a live price at or below the cap. We ranked each by how much usable capability a homeowner gets for the money, and we flagged brand support risk.

cards.label: Corded
cards.text: Constant power, no battery fade and no battery to age. The cord limits reach and the tool is louder. The Eastvolt is corded.

cards.label: Cordless
cards.text: Mobile, quieter and easier to handle. Battery fades under heavy use. The AOBEN, SEYVUM, Seesii and Kwionsi are cordless.

howToChoose.note: Choose corded for the garage and cordless for roadside and driveways.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: At least 300 to 400 ft-lbs of believable peak torque, a 1/2-inch drive and impact-rated sockets. Torque the nuts to spec by hand.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The AOBEN and SEYVUM are the sensible picks, the Seesii adds a second battery, and the Eastvolt is the corded option. The Kwionsi is too small.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You work on rusted suspension parts or need parts and battery support for years. A major brand tool outlasts any of these.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You change tires twice a year. The SEYVUM or Eastvolt is enough.

maintenance.why: Chrome sockets crack under hammer blows. Impact sockets are softer and safer.
An impact wrench overtightens nuts and warps rotors.
Small motors heat fast, and a rest protects the windings.
A worn anvil rounds sockets and slips.

faq.q: Can a budget impact wrench remove lug nuts?
faq.a: Yes, in most cases. Lug nuts are tightened to about 80 to 100 ft-lbs, and a believable 450 ft-lbs peak tool such as the AOBEN removes them. Rusted nuts may need penetrating oil.

faq.q: Why are torque claims so high?
faq.a: Peak breakaway torque is measured in different ways by each maker, and small brands choose the best-looking number. Claims over about 600 ft-lbs on a compact tool should be treated as marketing.

faq.q: Can I use these to tighten lug nuts?
faq.a: Use the wrench to run the nuts on, then finish with a torque wrench. Impacts overtighten nuts and can warp rotors.
Corded gives constant power and no battery cost. Cordless is more convenient for work away from an outlet.

faq.q: What size socket should I buy?
faq.a: Impact-rated 1/2-inch sockets in 17, 19, 21 and 22 mm cover most cars. Buy deep and standard lengths.
For small bolts and bikes, yes. For lug nuts it is not reliable, so choose a 20V-class tool.
